newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean won ends up, strikes a mid-term hazard.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean won ends up, strikes a mid-term hazard.

text.p: The won ended Wednesday's trading slightly higher on expectations that the central Bank of Korea would support the domestic currency, traders said.
Dealers said the central bank has pumped dollars into the market to brake the won's decline, but the bank has never acknowledged stepping into the market.

They added the won would continue to be pressured in the mid-term by fears that on-going strikes would further jack up the nation's trade deficit. The won ended at an intraday high of 848.90, against the day's opening rate at 849.00. It touched a six-year low of 849.40.

"Strikes could be harmful to the trade deficit," said a European bank dealer. "There are usually huge export negotiations in March. But this year, as strikes are hurting production at big exporters, this could be affected."

"I don't see the strikes impacting the dollar/won trading right now, but around February or March, when the export negotiations start, the effect of production slowdowns will be felt," a local bank dealer said.
The Bank of Korea has forecast this year's trade deficit at about $15 billion, against a $20 billion shortfall in 1996.
Dealers said that the central bank was expected to keep trying to stop the won from falling below the 850 level.
"The dollar's topside is very heavy at 849.50 to 850, where BOK intervention is expected," said the local trader. "So everyone wants to liquidate their long positions before that level."
The European bank dealer put Thursday's trading at 849-850, while the local bank trader put it at 848.50-849.50.
The base mid-rate was expected to be pegged at 849.10, compared to Wednesday's 848.30.
